messages.author: e1b933a0d5bbe14f
messages.subject: R and time
parts:
When working with very large corpora like the BNC, loading each file one by one and doing even the simplest operations takes hours to execute. I had one program running recently and after two days it was only at 50%, at which point I needed to stop it.

So my question is: are there any tricks or tips for increasing speed, or at least not wasting time? For example, outputing a progress counter can make a program take considerably longer (though I'd rather live with that one than to have an un-updated screen displaying for hours or days on end). Sometimes the same results can be achieved by different techniques; any rules of thumb regarding which ones are more speed-efficient?

Also, can R access the system clock? Sometimes I'd like to record how long a certain procedure. I'm not looking for millisecond comparisons.

--

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] R and time
parts:
Hm, I have done concordances on the BNC and considerably larger
corpora with R in a fraction of that time (on not great computers).
Without knowing what exactly you mean by "even the simplest
operations" it's hard to give specific advice.
> any rules of thumb regarding which ones are more speed-efficient?

The two main rules:
(1) wherever possible vectorize (rather than using loops)
(2) define collecting data structures whose size you know in advance
as having that size. For example:
freq.collector <- numeric(length=4054)
> Also, can R access the system clock?

Of course:
?date
?Sys.time

STG

messages.subject: RE: [CorpLing with R] R and time
parts:
Another solution would be to use multiple small writes to one file-write handle rather than appending to that file every time. I haven't ever done this, so caveat lector, but the import of section 6.2 of the R Data Import/Export manual (http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-data.html#Output-to-connections ) is that would be possible to open a file connection before the loop; then loop across all your input files writing the altered data to this single file connection WITHOUT having to do any reads of the output file; and then close after the end. This would save you the overhead of reading that increasingly huge file on every loop, and would be the typical way to do it in other programming languages, I think, esp. Perl and the like. (Also saves you from going to the command line and using unix shell tools as per Stefan’s other suggestion.)

 

best

 

Andrew.

Just to follow up:

I've been looking at some of my current and past scripts with an eye towards speed issues. Essentially, some were scripts for working with a small corpus which I copied, pasted and edited for BNC work. The issue of outputing to a file was in there, as mentioned, but I think the bigger issue was using strapply to split the text into <w...></w> lines, and doing that for 4000+ files. I just modified with the clunkier but more speed efficient method of GSUBing a unique string and STRPLITing at that point. Along with some other minor clean-ups, the whole thing just took 65 minutes to execute as opposed to hours or days.

Out of curiosity, is there any reason why strsplit has to consume? Seems to me a consume=FALSE switch would make r-life much more easier.

messages.author: f69dac69a9d51c10
messages.subject: RE: [CorpLing with R] R and time
parts:
Here's a log of an R session of mine to illustrate the difference in speed of strapply and gregexpr.

> mydata<-scan(file = file.choose(), what = "char", sep = "\n")
Read 4441 items #These are the 4,441 lines of Peter Pan (about 48,000 words)

> library(gsubfn)
Loading required package: proto

#Here are 4 lines of script prepared in the R editor and then moved across in one action to the R console
> starttime<-Sys.time()
> words<-unlist(strapply(mydata, "\\b\\w+\\b", perl = TRUE))
> endtime<-Sys.time()
> cat(endtime - starttime)
43.81339 #So, it took just over 43 seconds to put all the words into a vector

#Here's another 4 lines of script but this time using gregexpr to find the starting positions of all the words (and their lengths)
> starttime<-Sys.time()
> hits<-gregexpr("\\b\\w+\\b", mydata, perl = TRUE)
> endtime<-Sys.time()
> cat(endtime - starttime)
0.0765009 #Completes the job almost instantaneously

John

messages.subject: Re: R and time
parts:
On Nov 21, 12:36 pm, "Newman, John" <john.new...@ualberta.ca> wrote:
> Here's a log of an R session of mine  to illustrate the difference in speed of strapply and gregexpr.
>
> > mydata<-scan(file = file.choose(), what = "char", sep = "\n")
>
> Read 4441 items #These are the 4,441 lines of Peter Pan (about 48,000 words)
>
> > library(gsubfn)
>
> Loading required package: proto
>
> #Here are 4 lines of script prepared in the R editor and then moved across in one action to the R console> starttime<-Sys.time()
> > words<-unlist(strapply(mydata, "\\b\\w+\\b", perl = TRUE))
> > endtime<-Sys.time()
> > cat(endtime - starttime)
>
> 43.81339 #So, it took just over 43 seconds to put all the words into a vector
>
> #Here's another 4 lines of script but this time using gregexpr to find the starting positions of all the words (and their lengths)> starttime<-Sys.time()
> > hits<-gregexpr("\\b\\w+\\b", mydata, perl = TRUE)
> > endtime<-Sys.time()
> > cat(endtime - starttime)
>
> 0.0765009 #Completes the job almost instantaneously

Using perl = TRUE will cause strapply to use the slower R engine
whereas by default strapply uses faster tcl engine (if you don't
specify perl and if you have tcltk installed). See the ?strapply help
page. There is a link in the Links box on the gsubfn home page to
the tcl page that defines tcl regular expression syntax -- in most
cases its the same as in R but there are a few differences.

Also your gregexpr is only returning the positions and not the
contents so it would be expected to be faster in any case.

Also there is a faster limited version of strapply in development.
There is a benchmark of it on the gsubfn home page which shows it runs
the gsubfn-gries demo that comes with the gsubfn pacage 5x faster than
the current version of strapply (the difference would be even greater
if you compared it to the R engine. See the March 14, 2010 news item
on the gsubfn home page.) This version of strapply has not been
released yet.

The gsubfn home page is at http://gsubfn.googlecode.com

> Sorry. The March 14th news item refers to the speedup you get when you
> use the tcl engine rather than the R engine and that is already in the
> released version of the gsubfn package.  The speedups from the faster
> limited strapply are in addition to that.

Here is a comparison that to me seems fairer since it includes not
just the gregexpr but the entire computation that strapply does. We
read in James Joyce's Ulysses and collapse the first 10000 lines into
a string and then we run gregexpr/substring, strapply and the
unreleased strapplyc. Note that the current strapply using the
default tcl engine is only about 20% slower on this problem and the
unreleased strapplyc is about 40x faster than gregexpr/substring.
(strapplyc is not as general as strapply. It is hard coded to use the
function c.)

> library(gsubfn)
> joyce <- readLines("http://www.gutenberg.org/files/4300/4300-8.txt")
> joycec <- paste(joyce[1:10000], collapse = " ")
>
> # gregexpr/substring
> system.time({
+ ix <- gregexpr("\\w+", joycec)[[1]]
+ mapply(substring, ix, ix + attr(ix, "match.length") - 1,
+ MoreArgs = list(text = joycec))
+ })
user system elapsed
21.78 0.09 23.25
>
> # current strapply
> system.time(strapply(joycec, "\\w+"))
user system elapsed
28.00 0.06 29.73
>
> # unreleased strapplyc
> system.time(strapplyc(joycec, "\\w+"))
user system elapsed
0.68 0.00 0.69

Of course if you can find a special purpose function that does exactly
what you want then one would expect it would be faster yet but this
seems a reasonable price to pay for generality.

> system.time(unlist(strsplit(joycec, " ")))
user system elapsed
0.19 0.00 0.21

Kevin, here's what I use to time my large scripts:

start.time<-strptime(date(), format="%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y")

# a bunch of code and work R has to do here

end.time<-strptime(date(), format="%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y")

d<-difftime(end.time, start.time)

cat("The search took", round(d, 1), attr(d, "units"))
